questions.stem: In the ventricular action potential graphed here, the sustained plateau segment (phase 2) is maintained primarily by which ion movement?

explanation.summary: The plateau of the cardiac action potential reflects a balance in which inward L-type Ca2+ current offsets outward K+ currents, sustaining depolarization. Fast Na+ current drives phase 0, K+ efflux dominates phase 3 repolarization, and If pacemaker current operates in nodal cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The plateau of the cardiac action potential reflects a balance in which inward L-type Ca2+ current offsets outward K+ currents, sustaining depolarization. Fast Na+ current drives phase 0, K+ efflux dominates phase 3 repolarization, and If pacemaker current operates in nodal cells.

questions.stem: The upper tracing shows an abnormal depolarization arising during the prolonged plateau of the action potential. Which condition classically predisposes to this phenomenon?

explanation.summary: The top tracing depicts an early afterdepolarization (EAD), which arises from a prolonged plateau and is favored by QT-prolonging states such as hypokalemia and drug-induced long QT. The lower tracing is a delayed afterdepolarization (DAD), classically caused by intracellular calcium overload (e.g., digoxin toxicity).
explanation.whyCorrect: The top tracing depicts an early afterdepolarization (EAD), which arises from a prolonged plateau and is favored by QT-prolonging states such as hypokalemia and drug-induced long QT. The lower tracing is a delayed afterdepolarization (DAD), classically caused by intracellular calcium overload (e.g., digoxin toxicity).

questions.stem: In this four-panel sequence of AV nodal conduction, what event initiates the self-sustaining circuit shown?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A premature beat blocked in the fast pathway

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simultaneous conduction down both pathways at equal speed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Retrograde block of the slow pathway during sinus rhythm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced automaticity of a ventricular focus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete block of the AV node with a junctional escape

explanation.summary: AV nodal reentry begins when a premature beat finds the fast pathway still refractory, so it conducts anterogradely down the slow pathway. By the time it reaches the distal node the fast pathway has recovered, allowing retrograde conduction and establishment of a reentrant loop.
explanation.whyCorrect: AV nodal reentry begins when a premature beat finds the fast pathway still refractory, so it conducts anterogradely down the slow pathway. By the time it reaches the distal node the fast pathway has recovered, allowing retrograde conduction and establishment of a reentrant loop.

questions.stem: Arrhythmias originating from the lower labeled region of this heart typically produce which ECG finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absent P waves with a normal narrow QRS

choices.label: E
choices.text: A shortened PR interval with a delta wave

explanation.summary: Ventricular arrhythmias arise below the bundle of His, so activation spreads cell-to-cell rather than through the fast His-Purkinje system, producing a wide, bizarre QRS. Supraventricular arrhythmias arising above that level usually keep a narrow QRS unless aberrant conduction is present.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ventricular arrhythmias arise below the bundle of His, so activation spreads cell-to-cell rather than through the fast His-Purkinje system, producing a wide, bizarre QRS. Supraventricular arrhythmias arising above that level usually keep a narrow QRS unless aberrant conduction is present.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip was recorded in a patient on a Class IA antiarrhythmic with a prolonged QT interval. What is this arrhythmia?

explanation.summary: The strip shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that twist around the baseline, the hallmark of torsades de pointes, a complication of QT prolongation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The strip shows polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QRS complexes that twist around the baseline, the hallmark of torsades de pointes, a complication of QT prolongation.

questions.stem: The red tracing shows the effect of a Class IA antiarrhythmic on the ventricular action potential compared with normal. What ECG change would this altered action potential most likely produce?

explanation.summary: Class IA agents block Na+ (slowing phase 0) and K+ channels (delaying phase 3), lengthening action potential duration and repolarization, which prolongs the QT interval and predisposes to torsades de pointes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Class IA agents block Na+ (slowing phase 0) and K+ channels (delaying phase 3), lengthening action potential duration and repolarization, which prolongs the QT interval and predisposes to torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: This tracing shows a small change in phase 0 with a shortened action potential, typical of Class IB agents. These drugs preferentially bind sodium channels in myocardium that is in what condition?

explanation.summary: Class IB drugs (e.g., lidocaine) are selective for inactivated Na+ channels, which are abundant in depolarized ischemic myocardium, making them drugs of choice for ventricular arrhythmias after MI.
explanation.whyCorrect: Class IB drugs (e.g., lidocaine) are selective for inactivated Na+ channels, which are abundant in depolarized ischemic myocardium, making them drugs of choice for ventricular arrhythmias after MI.

questions.stem: The red tracing shows pronounced blunting of the phase 0 upstroke while action potential duration is unchanged, typical of Class IC agents. Which ECG finding results?

choices.label: D
choices.text: QT prolongation with a normal QRS

choices.label: E
choices.text: Marked QRS widening with unchanged QT

explanation.summary: Class IC drugs strongly slow phase 0 (conduction velocity) without altering repolarization, so the QRS widens markedly while the QT interval stays essentially unchanged.
explanation.whyCorrect: Class IC drugs strongly slow phase 0 (conduction velocity) without altering repolarization, so the QRS widens markedly while the QT interval stays essentially unchanged.

questions.stem: This diagram shows the fast-response cardiac myocyte action potential and its ion movements. The plateau (Phase 2) is maintained by a balance between which two opposing ion currents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calcium influx balanced by potassium efflux

choices.label: B
choices.text: Potassium influx balanced by sodium efflux

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sodium influx balanced by potassium influx

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sodium influx balanced by calcium efflux

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chloride influx balanced by calcium efflux

explanation.summary: During Phase 2, inward Ca2+ current through L-type calcium channels is offset by outward K+ current, holding the membrane at a plateau and prolonging the effective refractory period.
explanation.whyCorrect: During Phase 2, inward Ca2+ current through L-type calcium channels is offset by outward K+ current, holding the membrane at a plateau and prolonging the effective refractory period.

questions.stem: This figure depicts the three conformational states of the cardiac fast sodium channel. Class I antiarrhythmics bind with greatest affinity to which state(s), producing use-dependence?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The inactivated state only during diastole

choices.label: E
choices.text: All three states with equal affinity

explanation.summary: Class I drugs preferentially bind channels that are open or inactivated (states favored at fast heart rates), so blockade increases with rate, the basis of use-dependence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Class I drugs preferentially bind channels that are open or inactivated (states favored at fast heart rates), so blockade increases with rate, the basis of use-dependence.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a regular rhythm at a rate of approximately 43 bpm with an upright P wave of normal morphology preceding every narrow QRS complex. What rhythm does this represent?

explanation.summary: A regular rhythm below 60 bpm with a normal P wave preceding each QRS (normal PR interval and axis) indicates the impulse originates from the SA node at a slow rate, defining sinus bradycardia. A junctional rhythm would lack normal preceding P waves, and atrial fibrillation would be irregular with no discrete P waves.
explanation.whyCorrect: A regular rhythm below 60 bpm with a normal P wave preceding each QRS (normal PR interval and axis) indicates the impulse originates from the SA node at a slow rate, defining sinus bradycardia. A junctional rhythm would lack normal preceding P waves, and atrial fibrillation would be irregular with no discrete P waves.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip demonstrates narrow QRS complexes without preceding P waves at a rate of roughly 40-60 bpm. What rhythm is shown?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Complete heart block with ventricular escape

explanation.summary: When the SA node fails or is severely slowed, the AV junction acts as a subsidiary pacemaker firing at ~40-60 bpm. Because impulses travel down the normal His-Purkinje system the QRS is narrow, and P waves are absent (or inverted near the QRS) because there is no normal atrial depolarization from the SA node.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the SA node fails or is severely slowed, the AV junction acts as a subsidiary pacemaker firing at ~40-60 bpm. Because impulses travel down the normal His-Purkinje system the QRS is narrow, and P waves are absent (or inverted near the QRS) because there is no normal atrial depolarization from the SA node.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows normal sinus beats interrupted by an interval greater than 2 seconds with no atrial or ventricular activity, after which sinus rhythm resumes. What is the underlying mechanism of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abrupt failure of impulse formation by the SA node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Retrograde conduction from a ventricular focus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complete dissociation of atrial and ventricular activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Blocked conduction of atrial impulses at the AV node

explanation.summary: A sinus pause is an abrupt cessation of SA node automaticity, producing a flat line with no P waves or QRS complexes until pacemaker activity resumes. It reflects sinoatrial node dysfunction rather than AV conduction block, in which P waves would continue but fail to conduct.
explanation.whyCorrect: A sinus pause is an abrupt cessation of SA node automaticity, producing a flat line with no P waves or QRS complexes until pacemaker activity resumes. It reflects sinoatrial node dysfunction rather than AV conduction block, in which P waves would continue but fail to conduct.
